title: A Classroom Management Secret Top Teachers Use ers-use/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes an early-career mentor, a sixth-grade teacher named Chuck, whose students walked across campus in two calm, orderly lines and who commanded instant, silent attention the moment he entered a room. Other teachers dismissed Chuck's exacting attention to routines like walking in line as petty or unnecessary, but Linsin argues this dismissal misses a genuine secret to effective classroom management: how students perform everyday procedures, such as walking in a line or giving attention on request, is a direct and reliable measure of how well they will handle more consequential classroom demands like group work or receiving instruction. He rejects the idea that teachers can hold different behavioral standards for 'less important' activities and still expect strong behavior during instruction, arguing this sends confusing, inconsistent messages that set bad precedents. Instead, he frames simple routines like line-walking as a low-stakes 'learning lab' where students practice the same skills of following directions and respecting others that transfer directly into academic settings. He closes by inviting readers to test their own classroom management by observing how their students walk in line.
points: How students execute simple daily procedures like walking in a line is presented as a direct, observable measure of overall classroom management effectiveness.
Colleagues who dismissed a mentor's exacting standards for routines like line-walking as 'petty' were missing the real lesson embedded in those standards.
Holding different behavioral expectations depending on an activity's perceived importance sends a confusing message and undermines consistency.
A line of students reveals respect for the teacher and peers, ability to follow directions, and readiness to receive instruction.
Routine procedures function as a low-stakes 'learning lab' where students practice the same skills needed for success during actual instruction, without costing class time.
quotes: All 36 of them were walking in two perfect lines as Chuck followed from a distance of about 30 feet. They were calm and focused and walked with a casual purpose, displaying a level of maturity I had not seen before.

When I stepped inside the room, the student nearest me quickly got to his feet as he nudged the student next to him on the arm. His group, in turn, immediately dropped what they were doing, stood, and faced me.

You see, Chuck understood a secret to effective classroom management that so many others fail to grasp. The way your line looks when you walk across campus and the way in which your students give their attention when you ask for it... are measures of your classroom management effectiveness.

Having different behavioral expectations based on the importance of an activity doesn’t work because it sends a confusing message to students. Further, it sets a bad precedent, provides a bad example, and creates bad habits.
In effect, a line is a perfect learning lab, where students can practice the skills needed to be successful in the classroom—and without the loss of class time.
Watch closely because it accurately measures your classroom management effectiveness and, consequently, your effectiveness as a teacher.
